newsitem.title: USA: FOMC decision promises few answers for US markets.
newsitem.headline: FOMC decision promises few answers for US markets.

text.p: Despite the turbulent, rumor-ridden run-up to Tuesday's Federal Reserve policy meeting, economists are predicting only a modest reaction from U.S. markets when they finally get the central bank's decision on rates.

If the Fed does hike the federal funds rate by 25 basis points, as many in the market expect, a knee-jerk sell-off is likely. But most experts expect any price drop to be short-lived, especially in the long end of the Treasury yield curve, which could ultimately benefit from a rate rise.
Should policymakers decide to keep rates unchanged, a short-lived price rise would likely give way to concern at the long end that the Fed is behind the inflation curve.
Worries about the possibility of hefty hikes down the road would limit any immediate gains, leaving prices relatively unchanged, economists said.
"I think the only way we would see a major reaction in the markets is if the Fed surprised everyone by raising rates 50 basis points," said Christopher Low, senior economist at HSBC Markets Inc.

In a Reuters poll conducted last Thursday, 17 of 30 economists said they expected the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) to hike rates on Tuesday. However, only one of the 17 was calling for anything more than a 25 basis point rise.
Eight of the 12 regional Fed banks have submitted requests for a discount rate rise, indicating substantial pressure for tighter credit.

U.S. bond and stock markets have already priced in approximately 25 basis points of tightening. But even if the Fed does not raise rates on Tuesday, many analysts feel the market will anticipate a move at the FOMC's next meeting November 13.

"The belief is the Fed will either raise rates a quarter percentage point now or will do so after the election, so one way or the other you'll get the increase," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany .
Johnson said this scenario has complicated strategy for active portfolio managers trying to gauge the impact of Tuesday's policy decision on the markets.
Many longer-term investors, economists and forecasters are already looking past the meeting and asking themselves what lies ahead for monetary policy and economic growth in the fourth quarter.
Currently signals are mixed. Companies are stepping up production, rebuilding inventories and hiring workers, yet retail sales remain weak.
In any case, tight labor market conditions and rising wages -- the reasons many economists are predicting a hike in rates -- will not vanish on the heels of a 25 basis point fed funds boost.
As a result, the Fed's decision on Tuesday may raise more questions than it answers, economists suggested.
"My key question is where do we go after the meeting and I think that's really the relevant issue here," said Richard Berner, chief economist at Pittsburgh-based Mellon Bank.

"If the Fed goes as I expect they will, it seems to me questions will immediately arise as to when the next one will be and how many more there will be," he said. "The message might be that if they don't go (on Tuesday) then the chances are greater that they will need to go more forcefully down the road."
